story_text.value:
Hey HN! Today we’re releasing interfaze-1.1-lite, an open-weight model for tasks with a deterministic answer: OCR, STT with speaker diarization, classification and more.

Lite is a reasoning core plus a collection of specialist models (document reader, line detector, speech recognizer, segmentation). The core chooses the specialists to be executed and produces the answer in your JSON schema.

The specialist models give you: bounding boxes, word timestamps and a confidence score per each line and word. The raw outputs are returned next to the answer so that you can filter based on that. E.g., post rows above 0.9 automatically and forward the rest to a human.

Runs on a single 80 GB GPU (e.g. H100) without any additional services.

Happy to answer any questions regarding the architecture, benchmarks and limitations.

title.value: Show HN: The first open-weight model for general deterministic task

hi hn, i'm joey, the founder of problems.dev.

agents are increasingly becoming the most important customers of products. but when something goes wrong, an agent doesn't file a support ticket or let anyone know what happened.

problems was built to change that. agents submit reports via an sdk built into mcp servers or clis, but also take error reports on agent status pages.

if you're building for agents or just want to learn more, glad to have a discussion below.

story_text.value:
# Intro

The goal of this software is to make it easy to get the plan that's in your head onto the page. Start with the outline then add details. Then more details. Then numbers: costs, time, quantities. Then organize and categorize with #tags. All the sums, graphs and pivot table functionality happens automatically in the Calcs, Timeline, Stats views. And everything looks nice without you having to format it.

Currently, it's all local, saved in your browser. Save your plan permanently by downloading the '.tsum' file. Open (upload) the '.tsum' to start working again. Everything happens in the browser. The files are stored where ever you like. The '.tsum' file is just text - human and AI readable. Use it to plan anything. We hope it works like your brain does - by organizing things in trees.

# Story

This software is entirely vibe-coded. It had to be - none of my developer friends would help me out. The front end JS on this app is too complex for a part time developer like myself. I've had this idea for a while and was only able to bring it to life because of AI. It may not gain traction, but at least I can put it out there, use it myself, or stop thinking about it altogether. It's amazing to see it and actually use it - to know if my idea was good or not, at least for me. And I'm actually happy with it and have been using it. If you have thoughts about the idea, feel free to let me know. I'm open to suggestions for improvement.

# Disclaimer

This tool is mainly intended to help with project planning. But it can be used for any data that looks more like a tree than a table. Creating a quote or estimate for one-off projects is my favorite use case. The varying structure of costs across lumber, electrical, concrete and labor fits well.

Obviously, it doesn't replace all the many things Excel can do. It tries to improve on MS Project by making it easier to get your schedule on the page by coding into an editor instead of poking at menus in a GUI. It is still a proof of concept at this point, not a bullet-proof software package. If there's interest, it will be developed further. For now, it's good enough for me.

# Roadmap

I want this software to be the Excalidraw of Excel: free, simple, browser-based and fun to use. There are great things that Excalidraw does that would require servers and more costs. These features could be turned into a paid product if there is interest. So, if you're interested, please let me know: treesum.app (at) gmail.com.

# Thanks HN

This project would not have been possible with out AI. But also not without HN. Reading HN nearly every work day really shapes how to think about software and presenting it to people - especially for someone who is not a full-time developer. It's a great community and I've happily been a member since (at least) 2013.

title.value: Show HN: Treesum – Replace MS Excel/Project with a Code Editor

story_text.value:
(TLDR at the end)

Hello everyone,

I've been a gamer all my life, and ever since I got a Mac, I've noticed that I am unable to save recordings of gaming sessions the way NVIDIA ShadowPlay or other related software does on PC, but now it's possible.

The idea of how it works came from my PS4, which let me save clips, and I didn't know how it worked. I later looked into it and figured it out using a rolling buffer so you don't store everything, but just enough to capture the moment

The first version of this was built on iOS, and it's live on the App Store for you to check out. I am sure those who play Fortnite or Call of Duty: Mobile will want to check this out and share their clips with their friends. The macOS version was built back in April but I've slept on it for a while and decided to look into it and make it much faster, better and with much more customizability.

I'd really love your feedback, and I do appreciate contributions to the repo so we can make it better

TLDR: When gaming on Mac, you can now save moments you missed using a shortcut ;)

title.value: Show HN: Mac equivalent of Nvidia ShadowPlay. Recording missed moments on Mac

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Kirill.

A dozen coding agents running in parallel, producing walls of suggestions, comments and ideas, all at once, all crammed into 88 columns of terminal scrollback, all gone the moment you run the next command. Does this sound familiar?

FolderMd (https://foldermd.com) might be for you. It's free, and it's fast, and your agents can use it. I made it because I just couldn't handle it anymore.

It's a small Mac app that gives those documents a home. Agents read our explainer and then learn to write markdown into a .foldermd/, instead of writing it into the terminal. FolderMD then opens each one instantly and renders it like a book: real typography, syntax-highlighted code, Mermaid diagrams, light and dark mode.

You can edit a doc and save it, you can then add comments just like you would in Google Doc, and pass those comments to the agent.

Let me know what you think, and if you want to see any features, and improvements. Thanks! -K.

title.value: Show HN: Mac Markdown reader for your AI agents

story_text.value:
I work in a dark room a lot, and even the lowest keyboard backlight setting on my MacBook was too bright. I noticed macOS fades the backlight all the way to zero when it turns off, but the lowest level it lets you pick is noticeably brighter than that.

Lowlight is a small menu bar app that adds extra steps under the macOS minimum, plus the normal range above it. You choose how many extra steps you want. It fades the backlight down and holds it at the step you pick. If you change the keyboard brightness in Control Center, macOS takes back over.

It uses private CoreBrightness APIs, so a future macOS update could break it. It's Apple Silicon only, needs macOS 26, is signed and notarized, and is MIT licensed. You can build it from source with ./build.sh.

I'm happy to answer questions about how it works, or to hear about other Macs it does or doesn't work on.

title.value: Show HN: Lowlight – Dim your MacBook keyboard backlight below the macOS minimum

story_text.value:
I made a text/language identifier today, in a single C file, with no ML.

It classifies a text by checking which reference text a hand-rolled greedy LZ77 compressor finds least surprising. Each class is just a file of reference data. For a query, it sums the bits the compressed output would cost against each reference, and the cheapest one wins. It never writes a compressed file.

I got this idea after watching 3b1b's compression is intelligence series for the 3rd time, so i had to make sure i understand it finally.

I have my intro to C exam tomorrow, so feedback on the C is welcome.

title.value: Show HN: Surprisal – a language identifier in ~250 lines of C. No ML,no training

story_text.value:
Agents ignore AGENTS.md mid-session.

Then you tell them: hey, this is written in AGENTS.md.

- "You're absolutely right!" (proceeds with fixing)

But not anymore! This is a tool that would check the code immediately with a classifier (Jev etc.) and give the agent advice in the same turn.

It catches some mistakes that are difficult to put into lint rules and excels at the cases when semantic understanding is required - e.g. field names/types in a nested structure that contradict each other (more commonly known as "invalid states") (that we strive to make, e.g. "unrepresentable", some would say)

Even reviewer agent loops won't do much (as Primeagen's X post a month ago shows in all the colours [which I don't know if I can or can not link, and will stay on the safe side of not doing so]). This may or may not have an influence in nerd sniping me into writing that tool.

In cases like these, Hapsland (or its approach, at least) comes to help.

I know, I know, Abide (look it up!) exists, but I wanted (a) semantic expansion of code (b) full control over what's sent to Jev (hey, their ToS aren't that privacy-friendly) (c) less footprint on the file system. So I made it compatible. In case you want to use both, I mean.

TLDR: catch a change with a coding agent hook => expand it into semantic code structure, respecting privacy settings => call Jev with your own code semantic rules => deliver feedback to the agent in the same turn, in 0.5s.

P.S. This is a repost from last week when I was being a genius; I forgot to add "Show HN:" to the title, and then 30m passed and I couldn't delete that post anymore; renaming didn't put it into Show HN either.

title.value: Show HN: Hapsland – Realtime semantic advice on coding standards for the agents
